 gadget that measures acceleration, braking, and cornering and shows how smooth it all is on a little screen. i want something i can actually build and use while i'm learning to drive.

the hardware is a seeed xiao esp32s3, an mpu6050 motion sensor, and a small 128×64 oled. the xiao is tiny enough to fit inside the case and has usb-c for power and uploading code. the screen and sensor share an i2c connection, and there's one button for calibration and recording sessions. running off usb means no battery and no tapping into the car's wiring, which was the point.

the pcb is a 60×40 mm carrier board. the xiao sits in sockets, and there are connections for the screen, sensor, and button. the screen and sensor mount separately and hook up with short wires, so the case layout has more wiggle room. the sensor needs to stay flat even if the screen ends up somewhere else in the case.

one thing to be careful about when assembling is the connector pin order. the screen connector goes ground then 3.3v, and the sensor connector goes 3.3v then ground, so they're opposite and not interchangeable. both are labeled on the board and the assembly instructions call it out, but still check the wires against the labels on the actual modules before plugging anything in.

there are also two optional resistor spots for the i2c pull-ups. i marked them to stay empty by default, since the breakout boards might already have resistors on them. i need to look at the real modules before deciding if anything goes there.

the enclosure is a body, a removable lid, a screen clamp, two sensor clamps, a button plunger, and a separate button cap. the main case is about 90×76×34.4 mm, with the button sticking up a bit past that. it has four mounting points for the pcb and an opening for the usb cable. the screen sits behind a window in the lid and the sensor gets its own flat mount in the bottom.

a few mechanical problems came up in the design review and got fixed. some of the early clamp shapes overlapped other parts. the sensor supports had to move so they weren't sitting under the soldered header pins. the screen clamp needed room for its connector and wires. the usb opening had to be adjusted for the height of the xiao and its sockets. but these are all fixes to the computer model so far, so they still need checking with real parts.

the button has a guide and a travel stop now too. the printed plunger reaches down to the switch on the pcb, and the cap limits how far it can move. the actual switch height matters a lot here, so that's another measurement to take before i call the case dimensions final.

holding the button for 1.5 seconds and letting go starts calibration while the device is idle. after calibration, a short press starts a session and another short press ends it. letting go after a long hold shouldn't accidentally start recording. it shows forward and sideways acceleration, a moving dot, and a summary when the session ends. it also spits out csv over usb so i can look at the readings during bench testing. there are checks for failed sensor reads and bad calibration samples now, but those error cases haven't been tried on real electronics.

the automated results are a decent starting point. the firmware builds for the xiao board, and the motion, button, and calibration tests pass. the pcb checks report no electrical-rule or layout-rule violations and nothing unconnected. all seven printable parts have closed meshes, and the modeled fit checks pass. but that only checks the files and the software logic. it can't tell me if a module that shows up is a slightly different size, or if a printed part actually fits.

the repo has the editable kicad files, fabrication exports, stl files, step files, renders, and assembly instructions. the images attached are the assembled case render, an exploded view showing the inside, and the pcb layout.

the budget isn't finished. i have supplier listings for the main electronics, but connectors, screws, printing, pcb fabrication, shipping, and tax still need to be added up yk

next up is measuring the real components, going through the wiring, and testing the electronics on a bench before anything goes in the case. after that i can print the enclosure and check screen clearance, usb access, button movement, and whether the sensor mount is solid. so for now drivedot has a first set of design files, and the physical building and testing is still ahead!
